title: Apify API Tokens, Rate Limits and Errors in 2026
summary: The Apify API authenticates with personal tokens sent as bearer headers. It integrates with workflow tools like Activepieces and HTTP clients.
body_markdown:
## Stage 2: Run an Actor and read its dataset


Four calls, in order, run an Actor. Each one can fail in a way the previous one hides: **a started run isn't a finished run** , and a finished run isn't yet your data.


Here's the sequence the next four subsections walk through, with the points where production code has to branch.


1. ` POST /v2/acts/{actorId}/runs` with the Actor's input as the JSON body.
2. Read the run` id` and` defaultDatasetId` from the response.
3. Poll` GET /v2/actor-runs/{runId}` until` status` is` SUCCEEDED` .
4. ` GET /v2/datasets/{id}/items` to pull the results.


Everything that follows is about what to do when a step doesn't return what you expected.


### Start an Apify Actor run with POST


Send the Actor's input as the JSON body to` POST /v2/acts/{actorId}/runs` , with your token in the` Authorization` header. A successful call returns immediately with a run object in an initial state, not with results, so treat the response as a receipt.


Store two fields from it straight away: the run` id` and the` defaultDatasetId` . If your process crashes after the POST but before you save them, you have a run billing in the background that you can't find again, so persist both before doing anything else.


Decide up front what a failed POST means. A rejected input is a bug to fix, while a rate-limit or server error is worth retrying with backoff. Retrying blindly can start a duplicate run, so log the attempt before you repeat it.


### Poll Apify run status and fetch dataset items


Call` GET /v2/actor-runs/{runId}` on an interval and read` status` .` SUCCEEDED` is the only state where the dataset is complete.


Treat` FAILED` ,` ABORTED` and` TIMED-OUT` as terminal errors that need handling, not as reasons to keep waiting. A loop that only checks for success will spin forever on a run that has already died.


Add a ceiling to the loop, so a stuck run surfaces as your error rather than a hung worker. Once the status is` SUCCEEDED` , call` GET /v2/datasets/{id}/items` using the saved` defaultDatasetId` .


Large datasets come back in pages, so request them with offset and limit parameters and keep going until a page returns fewer items than you asked for. Reading one page and stopping silently truncates your results.


### Apify sync endpoint, polling or webhooks compared


Use polling as the default, the synchronous endpoint for short runs, and webhooks when runs are long and you have a public endpoint to receive them.


Approach Latency Reliability for long runs Code needed


Synchronous endpoint Lowest for quick runs, since one request returns the result Weakest, because the HTTP connection must stay open and can drop or time out Least


Polling Delayed by your poll interval Strong, because state lives on the server and you can resume Moderate: loop, ceiling, error branches


Webhook Near-immediate once the run ends Strong, provided your receiver is up and you handle redelivery Most: a reachable endpoint and verification


Losing the connection on a run that was fine is how the synchronous call fails, and it is the failure you can least afford.


A webhook removes polling traffic but moves the failure to your receiver, so pair it with a status check as a fallback.


### Official JavaScript and Python clients


Starting a run, waiting for it to finish and iterating dataset items are all wrapped by Apify's official JavaScript and Python clients. They also retry some failed requests for you, which removes much of the boilerplate above.


Check what the client retries and what it hands back to you, because a wrapped call can still end in a` FAILED` run that your code must inspect.


The clients save you from writing the loop. They don't decide what a failed run should mean for your pipeline.


If nobody on the team writes code, the same calls are available another way. The[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/) Apify integration runs an Actor and fetches its dataset items with the same API token, so a non-coder gets the start, wait and fetch sequence inside a workflow.


It is one of 746 integrations counted from the MIT-licensed open source monorepo, and each run leaves a trace you can read, so integration choice doesn't constrain your architecture.
